title: Robots Never Lie

hints.content: Read the whole file, including the comments at the bottom.

writeup.summary: The flag is hidden within an unindexed comment block at the bottom of the robots.txt file.
steps: 1. Inspect the provided robots.txt attachment in a plain text editor or browser.
2. Scroll past the standard User-agent disallow directives to the final comment section.
3. Extract the flag embedded in the internal comment: CTF{r0b0ts_t3ll_n0_l13s}.

title: Strings Attached
description: Our intern dumped the firmware of a mysterious device. It is mostly gibberish, but humans (even careless ones) leave readable text behind. Extract the key from the binary.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: There is a classic Linux command that prints readable sequences from binary files.

writeup.summary: A compiled device firmware dump contains unencrypted ASCII strings left behind in the binary image.
steps: 1. Analyze the binary firmware file firmware.bin using the UNIX strings utility.
2. Filter printable sequences for the competition flag format: strings firmware.bin | grep CTF.
3. Retrieve the exposed flag: CTF{str1ngs_4tt4ch3d_t0_b1n4ry}.

writeup.summary: Authentication audit log leak where an administrator accidentally submitted the flag string in an authentication field.
steps: 1. Inspect auth.log by searching for anomalous credential patterns or flag signatures.
2. Run grep "CTF" auth.log or examine unusual failed SSH/PAM login usernames.
3. Identify the anomalous username carrying the flag: CTF{l0g_l34k_k3y_f0und}.

title: Dead Code Walking
description: Running this script only prints a boring status message. But a function inside it is never called. Read the code, understand what the hidden function does, and find the key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Nothing forces you to run the script the way its author intended. You can call functions yourself, or re-implement the logic.

writeup.summary: A Python helper script containing an uncalled internal function that yields the flag when executed directly.
steps: 1. Inspect helper.py to identify definitions, hidden docstrings, or internal functions.
2. Observe the internal function _reveal() that is defined but never invoked in main.
3. Execute the function directly: python3 -c "import helper; print(helper._reveal())" to reveal CTF{pyth0n_d0cs_h1d3_s3cr3ts}.

title: Needle in the Access Log
description: 800 web requests, and only ONE of them does not belong. It comes from a client that is not a real browser and it is carrying something strange in its query string. Find the clue, then make sense of it to get the key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Every normal visitor looks like a browser. Look for the User-Agent that does not. The value it carries is encoded, not encrypted.

writeup.summary: A web server access log contains a rogue user agent transmitting an exfiltrated base64 telemetry payload.
steps: 1. Analyze access.log by filtering User-Agent strings to locate anomalies.
2. Identify the non-standard User-Agent "Beacon/0.9" transmitting a query parameter t=...
3. Base64-decode the extracted t parameter to recover the flag: CTF{n33dl3_1n_th3_l0g_st4ck}.

title: Metadata Never Sleeps
description: The picture says there is nothing to see, and the pixels agree. But every file carries a hidden passport of information about itself. Find the clue in the file's own data, not in the image.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Metadata viewers (exiftool, pngcheck, online EXIF viewers) show chunks that image viewers hide. strings alone will not be enough.

writeup.summary: Forensic PNG inspection reveals a compressed auxiliary metadata chunk (zTXt / tEXt) containing the hidden key.
steps: 1. Examine evidence.png with deep metadata extraction tools: exiftool evidence.png or pngcheck -t evidence.png.
2. Locate the auxiliary text chunk named "Secret" stored in the file headers.
3. Read the chunk content to discover: CTF{m3t4d4t4_n3v3r_sl33ps}.

title: Russian Dolls
description: Follow the trail of breadcrumbs. Each layer points to the next, and the final layer holds more than one candidate. Only one of them is the real key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Read every note. The real flag file is named exactly what you would expect.

writeup.summary: Nested zip archive steganography requiring multi-layer decompression to separate the authentic flag from decoy files.
steps: 1. Extract the primary container breadcrumbs.zip to find inner.zip.
2. Decompress inner.zip to obtain core.zip.
3. Extract core.zip and inspect flag.txt (ignoring misleading decoy notes) to obtain CTF{z1p_1n_z1p_1n_z1p}.

title: Silent Whitespace
description: An innocent-looking office memo. Read it a hundred times and you will find nothing. The secret is in what you cannot see at the end of each line. Do not open it in an editor that trims whitespace. Find the clue, then find the key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Two invisible characters, 8 per line. Think binary. Each line carries exactly one character. Use xxd/cat -A to reveal them.

writeup.summary: Whitespace steganography encoding binary bits (space = 0, tab = 1) at the end of text document lines.
steps: 1. Inspect memo.txt with hidden character visualization: cat -A memo.txt or xxd memo.txt.
2. Notice 8 trailing whitespace characters per line: space represents binary 0, tab represents binary 1.
3. Convert each 8-bit byte into ASCII characters across the first 40 lines to construct CTF{wh1t3sp4c3_h1d3s_wh4t_y0u_c4nt_s33}.

title: Least Significant Secret
description: A pretty gradient. Beautiful, harmless, and lying to you. Somewhere in its pixels, the smallest possible change in one colour channel is spelling out a message. Find the clue in the noise, then recover the key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Only the least significant bit matters. Tools like zsteg or StegSolve are your friends. Start with the red channel, row by row.

writeup.summary: LSB (Least Significant Bit) steganography hidden within the red color plane of a PNG image.
steps: 1. Analyze sunset.png using steganography analysis tools such as zsteg or StegSolve.
2. Inspect the least significant bit of the red channel (b1,r,lsb,xy) read in row-major order.
3. Extract the null-terminated ASCII string: CTF{l34st_s1gn1f1c4nt_b1t_l34k}.

title: Sixty-Four Gates
description:
The first gate of the Decode Chamber opens with a very common encoding. Decode this and enter the chamber:

Q1RGe2I0czNfczF4dHlfZjB1cl8xc18zNDV5fQ==

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: The alphabet is A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, / and the string may end with =.

writeup.summary: Standard Base64 encoding decoding challenge.
steps: 1. Identify the Base64 character set [A-Za-z0-9+/=] in the challenge description.
2. Decode the ciphertext using base64 -d or CyberChef.
3. Obtain the flag: CTF{b4s3_s1xty_f0ur_1s_345y}.

title: Hex Appeal
description:
Machines love hexadecimal. People do not. Turn this back into text:

4354467b6833785f74305f743378745f64306e337d

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Every two hex digits are one ASCII character.

writeup.summary: Hexadecimal byte representation of ASCII characters.
steps: 1. Recognize pairs of hex digits (base 16) in the challenge prompt.
2. Convert hex pairs to ASCII using xxd -r -p or CyberChef (From Hex).
3. Obtain the flag: CTF{h3x_t0_t3xt_d0n3}.

title: Thirteen Steps
description:
An ancient, symmetrical cipher guards this door. Apply it once to lock, apply it again to unlock.

PGS{e0g_gu1eg33a_e0px5}

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Look at the first four characters. What should they be?

writeup.summary: ROT13 Caesar substitution cipher rotating alphabetic characters by 13 positions.
steps: 1. Identify the ROT13 structure where punctuation, braces, and digits remain untouched.
2. Rotate alphabetic characters by 13 positions: tr "A-Za-z" "N-ZA-Mn-za-m".
3. Recover the flag: CTF{r0t_th1rt33n_r0ck5}.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Groups of 8 bits make one byte.

writeup.summary: Binary ASCII encoding where 8-bit clusters represent individual ASCII characters.
steps: 1. Group the bitstream into 8-bit octets (bytes).
2. Convert each 8-bit binary value to its ASCII character equivalent.
3. Read the decoded flag: CTF{b1n4ry_b1ts_unl0ck}.

title: Emperor's Shift
description:
An emperor once hid his orders by shifting every letter by a secret amount. You are not told the amount. Digits and symbols were left untouched.

NEQ{n43d4c_h4d_s3c3}

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: There are only 25 possible shifts. Plaintext starts with CTF.

writeup.summary: Caesar cipher shift by 11 positions.
steps: 1. Notice the monoalphabetic substitution with preserved word structure.
2. Test possible shifts (1-25) or align the ciphertext prefix with "CTF" (shift -11).
3. Decrypt the remaining text to get: CTF{c43s4r_w4s_h3r3}.

title: Double Wrap
description:
One layer was not enough for the designer. Two were used. Unwrap them in the right order:

UEdTe2dqMF95NGwzZWZfYTBnXzRfY2Uwb3kzen0=

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: The outside layer is the one you can recognise by its alphabet. Peel it first.

writeup.summary: Two-stage layered encoding: Base64 outer layer wrapping an inner ROT13 ciphertext.
steps: 1. Peel the outer encoding by base64-decoding the challenge text.
2. Identify the intermediate string as a ROT13 cipher starting with "PGS".
3. Apply ROT13 to decode into the final flag: CTF{tw0_l4y3rs_n0t_4_pr0bl3m}.

title: One Byte Wonder
description:
This message was XORed with a single secret byte, then written in hex. You know the plaintext starts with CTF{.

697e6c51521a5875411953751b59751a44197548535e1957

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: XOR the first ciphertext byte with 'C'. The result is your key.

writeup.summary: Single-byte XOR encryption broken via known-plaintext attack.
steps: 1. Known-plaintext attack: XOR the first ciphertext byte with the known first flag character "C" (ASCII 67).
2. This reveals the single-byte key: 0x2A (decimal 42).
3. XOR every byte in the ciphertext with 0x2A to reveal CTF{x0r_k3y_1s_0n3_byt3}.

title: The Chamber Key
description:
A polyalphabetic cipher protects this vault. The repeating key is a six-letter word that describes exactly what you are doing right now. Digits and symbols are untouched and do not consume key letters.

FXH{jlk3q3v3_e1dk3v_xrn0qn3h}

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: The key is a verb, in capitals. It is also in the name of this section.

writeup.summary: Vigenere polyalphabetic cipher with repeating keyword DECODE.
steps: 1. Determine that the cipher is Vigenere with keyword derived from the hint ("DECODE").
2. Apply Vigenere decryption with key DECODE.
3. Recover the flag: CTF{vig3n3r3_c1ph3r_unl0ck3d}.

title: Cube Root of Evil
description: A tiny public exponent, a huge modulus, and a lazy developer who forgot to pad the message. The message is short. Maybe too short. Recover the plaintext from the RSA output in the attachment and enter it as the key.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: Ask yourself: what happens if m^e is smaller than n? Do you even need to factor n?

writeup.summary: RSA low public exponent attack (e = 3) without padding where m^3 < n.
steps: 1. Inspect rsa_output.txt: public exponent e = 3 and ciphertext c.
2. Notice that because m^3 < n, modular reduction never wrapped around (c = m^3 in integers).
3. Calculate the exact integer cube root of c: m = integer_cube_root(c) and convert m to ASCII bytes.
4. Obtain the flag: CTF{cub3_r00t_0f_3v1l_rs4}.

title: The Onion
description: Good encodings are like onions: they have layers, and they make you cry. This blob has been wrapped more than once, and it is not the same wrapper twice. Identify every layer, peel them in order, and reach the core. The attachment holds the blob.

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.content: After each decode, look at the alphabet of what you got. Uppercase+digits 2-7+= is a giveaway. The final result looks backwards.

writeup.summary: Four-layer onion encoding: Base32 -> Base64 -> Hex -> Reversed ASCII.
steps: 1. Layer 1: Base32 decode (recognized by uppercase letters and digits 2-7 with padding).
2. Layer 2: Base64 decode the resulting payload.
3. Layer 3: Hex to ASCII decode the string.
4. Layer 4: Reverse the final ASCII string characters.
5. Extract the flag: CTF{p33l_th3_0n10n_l4y3rs}.
